plan.chapterName: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 14: Differentiation of Functions of Several Variables
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional diagram pairing a shaded surface with a set of direction arrows and their projections onto the plane below. An upward-opening paraboloid, shaded cream at the left, blue across the right rim, and orange along its lower flank, is drawn with the z-axis rising through it, the y-axis running to the right, and the x-axis coming forward at the lower left. A black dot on the near face of the bowl is labeled P0 (x0, y0, z0) by a leader line to the right. Three kinds of arrows leave that dot: an orange one angling up and to the right along the steepest rise, a dark blue one angling down and to the left, and a pair of teal arrows lying along a teal curve that wraps horizontally around the bowl at constant height. Red and gray dashed drop lines carry the arrangement down to a small flat copy of itself on the plane, where the blue arrow is labeled minus grad f with the note Most rapid decrease in f, the orange arrow is labeled grad f with Most rapid increase in f, and the teal arrows are labeled Zero change in f, and a small square marks the right angle between the gradient direction and the level direction. Flattening the three directions into the plane is what makes that perpendicularity visible. The diagram illustrates how the directional derivative reaches its largest value along the gradient, its most negative value opposite the gradient, and zero along the level curve.

Elliptical top rim of the bowl (outline of the cut)

interactions.label: Direction angle θ from ∇f (degrees)
interactions.teaches: The directional derivative D_u f = |∇f| cos θ is maximal when u aligns with ∇f, zero along the level curve (θ = 90°, 270°), and most negative opposite the gradient (θ = 180°).

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Flattening the three surface directions into the horizontal plane reveals that the gradient is perpendicular to the level curve through P0.
Hovering ∇f, −∇f, or a teal level direction links each plane label to its arrow on the surface: maximum increase, maximum decrease, and zero change at P0.
Rotating the bowl shows that the level curve is a horizontal circle and that the gradient points radially outward in the xy-plane, not along the surface.

demo_steps.title: Steepest increase
demo_steps.narration: The moving arrow is aligned with ∇f: the orange up-slope arrow on the bowl and its plane projection point the same way, and the directional derivative hits its largest value |∇f|.

demo_steps.title: Zero change along the level curve
demo_steps.narration: Rotated 90°, the arrow now runs along the teal circle of constant height. The bowl does not rise or fall in this direction, so the directional derivative is exactly zero.

demo_steps.title: Steepest decrease
demo_steps.narration: At 180° the arrow opposes the gradient, matching the dark blue down-slope arrow, and the directional derivative reaches its most negative value −|∇f|.

demo_steps.title: Flatten to the plane
demo_steps.narration: Dropping everything onto the plane below leaves only the plane diagram, where the right-angle marker makes the perpendicularity of ∇f and the level direction unmistakable.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Surface: paraboloid z = 0.5(x² + y²) over the disc x² + y² ≤ 6.8 (radius ≈ 2.6), so the rim sits at z ≈ 3.4; axes span x,y ∈ [-3.4, 3.4], z ∈ [-2.6, 4.2]. +X points toward the viewer at lower-left, +Y to the right, +Z up — matching the source axis labels (z up with arrowhead, y right, x forward-left). P0 = (0.9, 1.8, 2.03) on the near-right flank of the bowl, drawn as a black dot ~0.09 radius; leader line goes right and slightly down to the text 'P0 (x0, y0, z0)' placed outside the bowl at about (0.3, 3.9, 1.7). ∇f at P0 = (x0, y0) = (0.9, 1.8), |∇f| ≈ 2.01; unit gradient direction in the plane is radially outward (0.447, 0.894). Surface arrows start at P0 and are tangent to the surface: orange steepest-ascent arrow along (0.447, 0.894, |∇f|) normalized, length ≈ 1.5, drawn up-and-right; dark blue steepest-descent arrow is its negation, drawn down-and-left, same length. Teal level-curve arrows are tangent to the horizontal circle of radius 2.01 at height z0 = 2.03, directions ±(-0.894, 0.447, 0), length ≈ 1.0; the full teal level circle is drawn on the surface at that height, visible wrapping around the front of the bowl. Plane diagram: a small copy of the same four arrows drawn on the horizontal plane z = -2.0, centered directly below P0 at (0.9, 1.8, -2.0), scaled to ~0.8 of the surface-arrow lengths, with a thin black quadrilateral outline enclosing them and a 0.18-unit square right-angle marker between the orange gradient arrow and one teal arrow. Dashed drop lines: red (#E03030) from P0 and from the orange arrow tip straight down to the plane; gray (#999999) from the blue and teal arrow tips. Directional-derivative formula for the interactive arrow: u = cosθ·ĝ + sinθ·t̂ where ĝ = (0.447, 0.894, 0) and t̂ = (-0.894, 0.447, 0); D_u f = |∇f| cosθ ≈ 2.01·cosθ. Palette: bowl inner/left cream #F7EFD9, upper-right rim blue #8FB8DC fading to #6E9BC8, lower flank orange #E8703A to #F09A6A, teal #1E8A7C, gradient arrow orange #EA6A2A, negative-gradient arrow dark blue #1F3E8C, axes and leaders black #000000, dashed red #E03030, dashed gray #999999, labels black serif italic for math.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the paraboloid with a ParametricGeometry or a lathe over r∈[0,2.6] with vertex colors interpolating cream→blue by azimuth and darkening to orange near the lower flank; render DoubleSide with slight transparency (opacity ~0.95) so the inside of the bowl reads. Draw the rim, level circle, and axes as Line2/LineMaterial fat lines so they survive at small scale. Arrows use ArrowHelper or custom cone+cylinder meshes so head size stays constant. Dashed drop lines via LineDashedMaterial with computeLineDistances(). All text labels (z, y, x, P0 (x0,y0,z0), ∇f, -∇f, 'Most rapid increase in f', 'Most rapid decrease in f', 'Zero change in f') as CSS2DObject HTML sprites anchored to their geometry so they stay upright while orbiting; hover highlight = raycast on arrow meshes, brighten emissive and bold the paired label. The plane-projection toggle should cross-fade opacity of the surface arrow group vs the flattened group rather than hard-cutting, and show the numeric D_u f readout near the plane diagram.

authoredContext:
Suppose the function z=f(x,y) is differentiable at (x0,y0) (the figure).

The ‖u‖ disappears because u is a unit vector. Therefore, the directional derivative is equal to the magnitude of the gradient evaluated at (x0,y0) multiplied by cosφ. Recall that cosφ ranges from −1 to 1. If φ=0, then cosφ=1 and ∇f(x0,y0) and u both point in the same direction. If φ=π, then cosφ=−1 and ∇f(x0,y0) and u point in opposite directions. In the first case, the value of Duf(x0,y0) is maximized; in the second case, the value of Duf(x0,y0) is minimized. If ∇f(x0,y0)=0, then Duf(x0,y0)=∇f(x0,y0)·u=0 for any vector u. These three cases are outlined in the following theorem.

The gradient indicates the maximum and minimum values of the directional derivative at a point.

An upward facing paraboloid in xyz space with point P0 (x0, y0, z0). From this point, there are arrows going up, down, and around the paraboloid. On the xy plane, the point (x0, y0) is marked, and the corresponding arrows are drawn onto the plane: the down arrow corresponds to −∇f (most rapid decrease in f), the up arrow corresponds to ∇f (most rapid increase in f), and the arrows around correspond to no change in f. The up/down arrows are perpendicular to the around arrows in their projection on the plane.

The figure shows a portion of the graph of the function f(x,y)=3+sinxsiny. Given a point (a,b) in the domain of f, the maximum value of the gradient at that point is given by ‖∇f(a,b)‖. This would equal the rate of greatest ascent if the surface represented a topographical map. If we went in the opposite direction, it would be the rate of greatest descent.

discrepancies: Bowl coloring is washed out: the source shows a strongly orange outer/lower half of the paraboloid with cream-to-blue only across the upper rim band, whereas the generated bowl is predominantly pale blue/white with only a small faint orange patch at the very bottom.

The ∇f (orange) and −∇f (blue) surface arrows are noticeably shorter relative to the bowl than in the source, where they extend well beyond the rim and across the bowl face, making them the visual focus; here they are small and crowded near P₀.
At the default state (θ = 0) the purple u arrow is drawn coincident with the orange ∇f arrow, visually hiding the gradient arrow that is the centrepiece of the source figure.

The source labels the surface-level teal tangent arrows and gradient only in the plane diagram; the generated adds a purple 'u' and 'D_u f = 2.01' readout on the figure (extra elements not in the source, though pedagogically reasonable).

The flattened plane outline in the source is an irregular polygon skewed around the arrow set with leader lines to three annotations; the generated quad is more regular and its leader lines from 'Zero change in f' attach less clearly to the teal arrow tips.
evaluation.notes: A well-built, genuinely 3D reproduction with correct paraboloid, level curve, gradient frame, dashed drop lines and a faithful flattened plane diagram plus strong interactions (angle slider, view toggles, guided steps, hover linking); main weaknesses are the washed-out bowl color scheme (missing the dominant orange exterior) and undersized/occluded gradient arrows at the default view.
action_items: Strengthen the bowl's vertex-color ramp so the lower/outer surface is saturated orange as in the source, with the cream-to-blue gradient confined to the upper rim band.
Lengthen the surface ∇f and −∇f arrows (and slightly thicken shafts) so they read as the dominant elements extending past the rim, as in the original.
Offset or slightly shorten the purple u arrow (or start step 1 at a small nonzero θ) so the orange ∇f arrow remains visible when u is aligned with it.
Add small ∇f / −∇f labels on the surface arrows or a legend so the surface arrow colors are explicitly tied to the plane-diagram labels.

Extra elements not in the source (purple u arrow, purple dashed drop line, 'D_u f = 2.01' readout label) add clutter around the already tight arrow cluster, though they support the interaction.
